c.tagline: Skyscrapers, lagoons, and West Africa's beating pulse.

taxi.fareNote: Official orange 'taxi compteur' cabs have meters in theory, but fares are usually negotiated or fixed by zone before departure — agree on a price upfront.

emergency.note: Response times can be slow and inconsistent; hotels and tour operators often keep more reliable direct emergency contacts.

hood_landmark.Riviera: Cap Sud Shopping Mall, Riviera, Abidjan

avoid.reason: Petty and violent crime — caution in Adjamé, Abobo and Yopougon; keep car doors locked in traffic

hood_desc: Abidjan's high-rise business and government district, packed with banks, offices, and international hotels — convenient for business travelers who want to be near meetings and the CBD's restaurants.
An upscale, leafy area with embassies, the university, and the lagoon-front Hôtel Ivoire — favored by diplomats and expats who want a quieter, greener base close to the Rue des Jardins nightlife.
Abidjan's buzzing dining and nightlife hub centered on the famous Rue Princesse — best for visitors who want to be in the middle of the city's restaurant, bar, and maquis scene.
A newer, fast-growing suburb east of Cocody with shopping malls, golf-course hotels, and gated residences — suited to longer business stays and travelers who prefer a quieter, more suburban setting.
Home to the international airport and Vridi/Port-Bouët beach — practical for overnight layovers or early flights, though further from the main business and dining districts.

water.note: Tap water is not reliably treated; visitors should drink bottled water.

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash to the driver or conductor on SOTRA buses and gbaka minibuses; bateau-bus ferry tickets are bought at the dock. Some routes are introducing a rechargeable SOTRA card, but cash remains the norm for most visitors.
transit.hours: SOTRA buses and bateaux-bus run roughly 5:30am-8:30pm; shared taxis (wôrô-wôrô), gbaka minibuses, and ride-hailing apps cover most late-night trips.
transit.note: The lagoon splits Abidjan into several communes linked by a handful of congested bridges, so locals and visitors alike often prefer the bateau-bus ferries to avoid Plateau-Treichville-Yopougon traffic.

train: SITARAIL Abidjan-Ouagadougou line (freight-focused; passenger service currently limited/suspended)
bus: Intercity coaches from Adjamé/Gare Routière to Yamoussoukro, Bouaké, San-Pédro
ferry: SOTRA bateau-bus lagoon ferries linking Plateau, Treichville, Yopougon, and Abobo-Doumé

transit.m: SOTRA city bus to Plateau/Adjamé (45-60 min)

tip.r: Round up or leave 5-10% at restaurants when service isn't already included; not expected for taxis or casual eateries.

food.name: Attieke with grilled fish
food.desc: Fermented grated cassava couscous served with a whole tilapia or capitaine grilled over charcoal, raw onion, tomato and fiery pepper sauce.

places.name: Maquis du Val
places.note: Well-known open-air maquis for grilled fish and chicken with attieke.

places.name: Allocodrome de Cocody
places.note: Famous open-air grill yard; dozens of cooks doing fish, chicken and plantain.

places.name: Maquis Chez Helene
places.note: Long-running maquis praised for its fish, meat and braised chicken.

food.name: Alloco
food.desc: Ripe plantain cut into chunks and deep-fried in palm oil until caramelised, salted and eaten with chilli-onion sauce and often a fried egg.

places.name: Allocodrome de Cocody
places.note: The alloco institution the neighbourhood is named for; go in the evening.

places.name: Marche d'Adjame stalls
places.note: One of West Africa's biggest markets; alloco and garba for pocket change.

places.name: Treichville street stands
places.note: Roadside braziers frying alloco to order all afternoon in the old quarter.

food.name: Kedjenou
food.desc: Chicken or guinea fowl slow-steamed in a sealed clay canari with tomato, ginger, aubergine and chilli, cooked in its own juices with no added water.

places.name: Le Tamarin
places.note: Elevated Ivorian cooking and service; a comfortable place to try kedjenou.

places.name: Restaurant Kajazoma
places.note: Neighbourhood restaurant serving the full range of Ivorian home dishes.

places.name: O'Good Food
places.note: Modern Ivorian kitchen that puts kedjenou and sauces on a written menu.

food.name: Garba
food.desc: The national street snack: chunks of deep-fried tuna piled on attieke with raw onion, tomato, chilli and a splash of oil, wrapped in paper.

places.name: Garba stands of Adjame
places.note: Market-district kiosks frying tuna nonstop; the cheapest real meal in Abidjan.

places.name: Yopougon garba kiosks
places.note: The city's biggest commune has garba shacks on nearly every corner.

places.name: Treichville street kiosks
places.note: Classic working-class garba spots near the market and the port.

food.name: Brochettes and grilled escargots
food.desc: Charcoal skewers of beef, mutton or chicken gizzards dusted with chilli-peanut spice, plus the Ivorian speciality of big grilled snails in sauce.

places.name: Espace 331
places.note: Reputed for the best grilled snail brochettes in the country.

places.name: Rue Princesse maquis
places.note: Famous nightlife strip lined with grills; late, loud and very local.

places.name: Maquis du Val
places.note: Skewers and braised meats alongside the fish, with cold beer.

food.name: Sauce graine with foutou
food.desc: Rich palm-nut stew with fish, crab or beef, eaten with foutou: pounded plantain and cassava rolled into a smooth ball and dipped by hand.

places.name: Restaurant Kajazoma
places.note: Full spread of Ivorian sauces, graine, claire and arachide, with foutou.

places.name: Maquis Chez Helene
places.note: Home-style sauces and pounded foutou in a relaxed maquis setting.

places.name: O'Good Food
places.note: Reliable sit-down version of the sauces for visitors new to the cuisine.

food.name: Bangui (palm wine)
food.desc: Naturally fermented sap tapped from palm trees, sweet and cloudy in the morning and increasingly sharp and alcoholic by evening.

places.name: Rue Princesse maquis
places.note: Maquis along the strip serve bangui by the bottle with the grills.

places.name: Marche d'Adjame
places.note: Vendors sell fresh-tapped palm wine straight from the delivery jugs.

places.name: Maquis du Val
places.note: Serves bangui alongside beer for a full traditional maquis meal.

food.name: Bissap and gnamankoudji
food.desc: Bissap is deep-red hibiscus infusion with mint and sugar; gnamankoudji is sharp fresh ginger juice with pineapple and lemon. Both sold ice-cold in bags.

places.name: Marche d'Adjame
places.note: Market women sell both juices frozen in sachets for a few francs.

places.name: Allocodrome de Cocody
places.note: Juice vendors work the grill yard, ideal with fried plantain.

places.name: Marche de Treichville
places.note: Reliable stalls for bissap, ginger juice and baobab drink near the market.

landmarks: St. Paul's Cathedral
This striking modernist cathedral rises above the Cocody lagoon with a sail-like silhouette that has made it Abidjan's most photographed religious landmark.
Hôtel Ivoire
This legendary lagoon-front hotel and its bowling alley, casino, and skating rink once symbolized Abidjan's 'Ivorian miracle' era and remain a beloved city icon.
Le Plateau Skyline
Abidjan's glittering business district skyline, especially lit up at night across the lagoon, earns the city its nickname 'the Manhattan of West Africa.'
Henri Konan Bédié Bridge
This sleek toll bridge spanning the Ébrié Lagoon connects Cocody and Marcory, offering dramatic views of the lagoon and skyline for photographers.
Grand-Bassam
This UNESCO World Heritage colonial town near Abidjan charms visitors with crumbling Franco-African architecture, palm-lined beaches, and a rich trading-post history.
Musée des Civilisations de Côte d'Ivoire
Housing masks, statues, and ceremonial artifacts from across Ivorian ethnic groups, this museum offers a deep dive into the nation's diverse cultural heritage.
Banco National Park
A rare stretch of primary rainforest inside a major African city, this park lets visitors hike among towering trees and spot monkeys minutes from downtown.
Treichville Market
A sprawling, sensory-rich market packed with textiles, produce, and crafts, this is where visitors experience the vibrant everyday pulse of Abidjan.
La Pyramide
This bold Brutalist pyramid-shaped office building in Le Plateau is one of Abidjan's most distinctive and photographed pieces of 20th-century architecture.
Cocody Town Hall
The striking modern city hall of Abidjan's affluent Cocody district stands as a landmark of civic architecture in one of the city's most scenic neighborhoods.

dom.op: Sitarail (Abidjan-Ouagadougou line) — tickets at Treichville station, no online booking

train.note: Sitarail runs one international line from Abidjan's Treichville station north through Bouaké and Ferkessédougou into Burkina Faso (Bobo-Dioulasso, Ouagadougou) - a very slow multi-day/overnight train with sleeping accommodation, historically a few times a week. Service has been intermittent and cut back because of the security situation in northern Côte d'Ivoire and Burkina Faso; tickets are sold at the station and Sitarail has no reliable public booking website, so confirm locally that the passenger train is running before you plan around it. The same line covers the only domestic rail (Abidjan-Bouaké-Ferkessédougou).

intl.op: Malian coach lines (e.g. Bani, Africa Tours Trans)

bus.note: International coaches to Burkina Faso, Mali, Ghana and beyond leave mainly from the Gare Routière d'Adjamé; there is no pan-regional online booking, so buy at the operator's counter and carry your passport and visas for each border. Operator names above are the usual carriers on these routes but should be confirmed on the ground.

ferry.note: No scheduled international passenger ferries - the Port of Abidjan is cargo and cruise only. Within the city, SOTRA and private companies run lagoon boat-buses (bateaux-bus) across the Ébrié Lagoon as everyday local transport.

full.name: Yamoussoukro
full.blurb: Ivory Coast's official capital, known for its grand basilica and wide boulevards.

full.name: Takoradi
full.blurb: Ghanaian port city known for its harbor, beaches, and offshore oil industry.

full.name: Sekondi-Takoradi
full.blurb: Twin port city on Ghana's coast known for fishing, harbors, and oil industry growth.

full.name: Divo
full.blurb: Ivorian town known for cocoa and coffee farming in the country's forested south.

full.name: Gagnoa
full.blurb: Inland Ivorian town known as a center of the region's cocoa farming.

full.name: Abengourou
full.blurb: Cocoa-growing city in eastern Côte d'Ivoire known for its agricultural markets and local culture.
